properties.evidence: The three facets of that idea are all clauses that would go into this interface's spec; settling this first gives them somewhere to be written down, and settling them first leaves the same question open for the next tool.

How a client composes a beamline cannot be shaped until this is settled — a declarative spec the server turns into xrt calls and an exec of agent-written Python are different capabilities, not two implementations of one.
Whether the server accepts a host file path, inline source, or only a curated set of known example scripts is exactly what this decision determines.

Defaulting everything makes a tool pleasant to call by hand, where the caller remembers what they omitted; it was applied without asking whether the caller would be a model assembling arguments from a schema, which has no such memory.

Taking every 20th point is a reasonable way to keep a printed table short, and it was chosen to keep the payload small for a reader; nobody asked what it does to a feature narrower than the new spacing, because nobody modelled the reply as data somebody would compute from.

Returning everything computed is the generous choice when a person will skim it and discard it; it becomes a standing cost only when the reader is a model that must carry the reply, and that reader was never the one being designed for.

Nothing in the design said what a response must look like, so each tool's return annotation was chosen for the convenience of writing that one function; the envelope and the missing schemas are what the SDK then derived from those unconsidered annotations.

Version and timestamp are properties of a response rather than of a computation, so with no requirement about what a response carries there was no place for them to be asked for; every tool was written to answer a physics question and each one did.
A meta block on every response makes every response bigger, which is the cost F3 is complaining about; both cannot be optimised at once and whoever settles one has to settle the other.

A wall-time estimate is only meaningful with the machine that produced it named, which is the provenance block the other idea proposes; without it the estimator returns a number whose applicability nobody can check.
Option (b) replaces the dict and list[dict] annotations that generate the inconsistent envelope and the null output schemas, so that finding closes as a side effect rather than needing its own fix.
That finding IS the absence of this node and its spec; recording the interface is the direct answer to it rather than to any one of its symptoms.
Facet (a) is precisely the missing thing that finding records: a version and a timestamp attached to the number that carries them.

Choosing to serve over streamable HTTP as well as stdio is what forces this question: a remote client reaching a server that executes supplied Python is arbitrary code execution on the xrt host. Over stdio alone it would be a much smaller question.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Claude's idea, 2026-09-16, not the trial's — offered because the trial's findings kept pointing at the same hole and this is the shape of a fix for the hole rather than for any one finding.

The design holds six components and zero Interfaces, and the one thing this project ships IS an interface. The idea: record the MCP tool surface as an Interface node with a real spec — what every response carries, what the envelope is, what a null means, what the payload budget is — and then the six findings stop being six opinions and become one contract that can be checked.

Three ways to do it, in increasing cost:
(a) Just the Interface node, spec in prose. Cheap, and it gives later sessions somewhere to look. Does not catch anything on its own.
(b) The node, plus typed pydantic result models on every tool so the SDK publishes a real output schema. This also fixes the envelope inconsistency and the two missing schemas as a side effect, because both come from `dict` and `list[dict]` annotations.
(c) (b) plus a test that asserts the contract — every tool's reply carries the meta block, no reply exceeds a byte budget, every envelope has the same shape. This is the only version that catches the seventh tool somebody adds in six months.

Counter-argument, and it is a real one: this is a proof of concept with one user, and (c) is the kind of scaffolding that is easy to justify and hard to earn. The honest version of the counter is that the cost of (b) is close to zero because the models have to be written anyway to get output schemas at all, while (c) only pays off if this outlives the demo.
properties.name: OPEN — should the tool surface itself be modelled as an interface in the design?
properties.rationale: Not from the trial. Offered by Claude on reading the trial's six findings and measuring what they had in common. Recorded as an idea, NOT as intent, and deliberately not acted on: whether a proof of concept deserves a contract is exactly the sort of call that belongs to Anthony and not to the person who would enjoy writing it.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Three facets, all from the xrt-demo trial, all pulling the same way: a response that describes itself.

(a) I1 — build provenance. Either a `server_info` tool returning xrt-mcp / xrt / Python versions and platform, or "better for provenance" in the trial's words, a small `meta` block on EVERY response carrying at least the xrt-mcp and xrt versions. Cheap either way. The trial prefers the per-response block and gives the reason: a tool you must remember to call is a tool that gets forgotten, and the version is only useful attached to the number it produced. Counter-argument worth keeping: a meta block on every response costs bytes in exactly the context window that finding F3 says is already too full, so this pulls against the payload-budget idea and the two should be settled together.

(b) I2's sibling, I3 — echo the sampled window next to every flux and power number: energy_min_eV, energy_max_eV and the angular half-acceptance. The server instructions already TELL the caller to report the window; putting it in the payload makes it impossible to quote the number without it. Cheap, and it is the one facet with no counter-argument I can find.

(c) I4 — a machine-readable reason for a null. `flux_ph_s: null` and `flux_ph_s: null, flux_null_reason: "geometric source carries no flux weight"` are the same to a person and completely different to a design that must separate "not verified" from "failed". Cheap. Note the trial has not yet seen what a trace actually returns here — it lists this as worth checking when it gets there, not as observed.

These can be answered separately, but one interface contract would settle all three at once.
properties.name: OPEN — what should a response carry besides the answer?
properties.rationale: Ideas from the xrt-demo trial log, 2026-09-16, relayed by Anthony. Recorded so they are not lost; NOT claimed as intent — nobody has chosen any of them. They matter more than their size suggests because they are the direct counterpart to the root cause: the server has no notion of a response as an object with obligations, and each of these is one obligation somebody noticed was missing.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The trial's I2: an `estimate_trace_cost(spec)` returning expected rays and wall time, so a caller can find out whether a trace breaches a budget without spending the minute to find out. The trial has real budgets on its box — 20,000 rays and 60 seconds — and says the only way to test them today is to run the trace.

What makes this more tractable than it sounds: cost here is dominated by source emission sampling, not by the optics. A geometric source is milliseconds whatever you hang off it; an undulator was measured at roughly 30 s for 20,000 rays on this machine and scales close to linearly in nrays. So the estimator does not need a model of the beamline at all — source kind, nrays and a measured per-ray constant would get most of the way.

What makes it harder than it sounds, and it is the interesting part: that per-ray constant is a property of the MACHINE, not of the design. An estimator calibrated here would be wrong on the work computer — which is the same two-machines problem the provenance idea exists to solve, arriving from the other direction. So either the estimator calibrates itself on first use and reports when it last did, or it returns ray counts only and leaves wall time to the caller.

A cheaper cousin worth considering beside it: return the actual elapsed time and ray count on every trace (trace_beamline already returns `seconds`) and let a caller build its own expectation from what it has seen. That needs no new tool and no calibration, and it degrades honestly on a machine nobody has measured.
properties.name: OPEN — should the server say what a trace will cost before running it?
properties.rationale: Idea from the xrt-demo trial log, 2026-09-16, relayed by Anthony. Recorded so it is not lost; NOT claimed as intent. The timing numbers quoted are measured on Anthony's Linux box during the build on 2026-09-16; the linearity claim is an expectation from how xrt samples emission and has NOT been measured across ray counts.

properties.decision: Treat this as a proof of concept. The goal is to establish that the capability exists and is worth having; deciding what it is FOR — which beamline, whose workflow, which problem — is deliberately left until after people have seen it. Questions that depend on a use case (where it is deployed, who operates it, what conventions the build follows) are set aside rather than guessed at.
properties.name: This is a proof of concept; the use case comes later
properties.rationale: STATED BY ANTHONY 2026-09-16: "I don't know the rest of the answers yet. I just think this would be a pretty cool capability to have and then we can figure out how to use it. For now, this is just a proof of concept." Recording it matters because it changes what counts as done: a proof of concept is finished when it is convincing, not when it is complete, and the long list of things this does not do (no wave propagation, four element types, stateless, no auth) stops being debt and becomes scope. It also means the open questions below are DEFERRED by a decision rather than forgotten.

properties.decision: DEMO TAKES CANDIDATE (b), STILL AWAITING ANTHONY'S WORD. The MCP surface accepts a declarative beamline description — source, optics, apertures, screens as typed data — which the server turns into xrt objects itself. The server never executes agent-supplied Python source. The other candidates were (a) trust it fully and keep the server local, and (c) sandbox traces in a subprocess.
properties.name: The agent sends a beamline spec, not Python
properties.rationale: RAISED AND THEN ANSWERED BY CLAUDE, 2026-09-16 — Anthony has NOT confirmed it, which is why this stays proposed. Why (b): running an existing script and composing a beamline both end in executing Python an agent chose or wrote, and Anthony asked for streamable HTTP as well as stdio, so (a) would hand anyone who can connect arbitrary code execution on the xrt host. (b) makes the question moot rather than managed — there is nothing to exec — it is the shape that survives the HTTP transport, and it gives the model a typed surface it can reason about instead of asking it to write xrt code blind. Cost: anything expressible in xrt but not in the spec is unreachable until the spec grows, which is the right failure mode for a demo because it fails visibly rather than silently. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE DESIGN: "run an existing beamline script" is NOT in the demo — under (b) it would mean a curated set of known-good templates, not arbitrary paths, and that is what the demo ships.

properties.description: The contract between this server and whatever calls it. It existed from the first commit and was not written down, which is the cause the first outside trial's six findings shared: with nothing saying what a response WAS, six return statements each invented their own answer. Recorded 2026-09-16 as the fix at the cause rather than at any of the six symptoms.
properties.name: The MCP tool surface
properties.spec:
Ten tools over MCP (json-rpc, stdio or streamable HTTP). The contract, as pinned by tests/test_contract.py:

1. EVERY TOOL DECLARES WHAT IT RETURNS. Results are pydantic models in results.py, so the published output schema is real. `dict` and `list[dict]` annotations are forbidden — the first produced no schema at all, the second made the SDK wrap the reply in {"result": ...} while the dict-returning tools went back bare, which is where the inconsistent envelope came from.

2. EVERY REPLY CARRYING A NUMBER CARRIES `meta`: {xrt_mcp, xrt, computed_at}. Three fields, because a version is only useful attached to the number it produced and a tool you must remember to call gets forgotten. The rest of the environment is one `server_info` call, because it does not change within a session.

3. CONTINUOUS PHYSICAL QUANTITIES ARE REQUIRED; DISCRETE CHOICES MAY DEFAULT. A defaulted crystal is a menu item you notice omitting. A defaulted energy silently substitutes a physics assumption and returns a well-formed plausible answer to a question nobody asked.

4. A NULL SAYS WHY. flux_ph_s from a geometric source comes with null_reason, so "cannot be computed from this source" is distinguishable from "the calculation failed".

5. BULK IS OPT-IN. A lookup reply stays under about 2 KB; arrays come only when asked for. An agent carries every byte of a reply for the rest of its session.

6. A SAMPLED QUANTITY TRAVELS WITH ITS WINDOW. Flux and power carry sampled_window, because they are only ever the flux and power inside it.

7. THRESHOLD-DEFINED QUANTITIES CARRY THEIR DEFINITION. cutoff_definition, edge_definition, size_convention. A cutoff energy without its threshold and polarisation is not a number.

8. UNITS LIVE IN KEY NAMES (energy_eV, pitch_mrad, darwin_width_urad), and dimensionless quantities are named so.

9. A SAMPLED CURVE IS NOT DECIMATED BELOW THE SCALE OF ITS OWN FEATURES. This one is written in blood: returning every 20th point of a reflectivity curve rendered three absorption edges as a single V-shaped notch that appeared to recover.

properties.name: ROOT CAUSE B: the consumer was imagined as a person reading the output once
properties.statement: Every payload decision in this server makes sense for somebody reading it once in a terminal and makes less sense for a model that must carry it for the rest of a session. A 1.3 KB reflectivity curve is free on a screen and is 84% of the payload in a context window (measured: 1278 bytes with the curve, 169 without). Twenty curve points are plenty to eyeball and lossy as data. A default energy is a kindness to someone who typed the call and knows what they left out, and a trap for a model that filled the call from a schema. Distinct from ROOT CAUSE A and not caused by it: an interface contract written with the same reader in mind would have specified the same 20-point curve and the same defaults. This is what explains F3, F5 and F6, and A explains F1, F2 and F4.

properties.name: F5: every lookup tool defaults every physical quantity, not just the discrete ones
properties.statement: MEASURED 2026-09-16 across all four instant-lookup tools: crystal_at_energy(crystal=Si111, energy_eV=9000), mirror_cutoff(coating=Rh, pitch_mrad=3.0), undulator_harmonics(period_mm=21.0, K=1.5, ring_GeV=3.0), crystal_energy_range(crystal=Si111). Not one required argument anywhere. The trial flagged energy_eV and called it a judgement call; the measurement shows it is not one tool's slip but a rule applied uniformly, which is what makes it a class. The distinction that was never drawn: a defaulted discrete choice (Si111) is one a caller notices omitting, because there is a visible menu; a defaulted continuous quantity (9000 eV, 3 mrad, K=1.5) silently substitutes a physics assumption and returns a well-formed plausible answer to a question nobody asked. Mitigating fact, which the trial also spotted: every one of these IS echoed back in the response, so the wrong assumption is visible to anyone who reads the reply rather than only the number.

properties.name: F6 is worse than reported: the 20x decimation turns an absorption step into a notch
properties.statement: MEASURED 2026-09-16. reference.mirror_cutoff computes reflectivity on 400 log-spaced points and returns energies[::20] — 20 points. Between 2900 and 3600 eV the reply keeps exactly ONE sample. The full curve there shows three step-downs, at 2998->3029, 3124->3156 and 3391->3426 eV, which match Rh's tabulated L3 (3004), L2 (3146) and L1 (3412) absorption edges to within the grid spacing. Reflectivity falls 0.97 -> 0.88 across them and then recovers only slowly, reaching 0.913 by 4206 eV and never returning to its pre-edge value in that range. The decimated reply shows 0.9715 at 2790 eV, 0.8850 at 3426 eV, 0.9126 at 4206 eV — which reads as a V-shaped dip that recovers. A user sizing harmonic rejection off that reply would conclude the mirror is back to normal above 4 keV. It is not. So the trial's reading was right in kind (real absorption edges, correct physics) and wrong in two details worth fixing: they are L edges, not M edges, and the shape they saw is an artifact of the sampling rather than the physics. This is a wrong conclusion reachable from a correct computation, which is the worst kind.

properties.name: F4 mechanism: the envelope is derived from the Python return type, not chosen
properties.statement: MEASURED 2026-09-16 by reading the generated tool schemas. `list_beamlines` is annotated `-> list[dict]`; the SDK cannot express a bare array as structured output, so it wraps it and publishes outputSchema {"properties": {"result": {"type": "array"}}, "required": ["result"]}. `crystal_at_energy` and `mirror_cutoff` are annotated `-> dict`; that is already an object, so the SDK wraps nothing — AND, because `dict` carries no field information, it publishes outputSchema null. So the trial is right that there are two conventions, and the natural reading (someone was sloppy with their JSON) is wrong: the envelope is a function of the return annotation. The more serious half is the one the trial could not see from the payloads — two of the three tools it called declare NO output schema, so a model has to call them to learn their shape. Both halves have the same fix: annotate tools with real pydantic result models instead of `dict` and `list[dict]`.

properties.name: F1/F2: nothing in a response says which build computed it, or when
properties.statement: CONFIRMED 2026-09-16. No payload carries an xrt-mcp version, an xrt version, a Python version or a timestamp, and there is no server_info tool to ask. The trial names the consequence precisely: it plans to run the same design on two machines and compare, and if the numbers disagree there is no recorded fact separating "different source model" from "different xrt build". This is the highest-cost finding of the six because it is not a defect in any answer — every number is right — it is that the answers cannot be USED as evidence later. A wrong number gets caught; an unattributable right one gets quoted for years. Worth noting what makes it urgent rather than tidy: xrt is at 2.0.0b1, a beta that will move under this server, so "which xrt produced this" is a question that WILL have different answers over the life of these records.

properties.name: F3: 84% of a mirror_cutoff reply is a curve nobody asked for
properties.statement: MEASURED 2026-09-16: mirror_cutoff("Rh", 3.0) serialises to 1278 bytes with the reflectivity curve and 169 without. The curve is 84% of the reply and is unconditional — there is no way to ask for just the cutoff number. The trial's framing is the right one: in a normal client this is harmless, in an agent client every byte lands in the context window and stays for the session, so a design session doing many optics checks pays for it repeatedly. The same question applies to scan_element, which returns a full table of swept values, and to trace_beamline, which returns a block per screen.

properties.name: ROOT CAUSE A: the seam was never modelled, so every response was shaped at its own return statement
properties.statement: This design has ZERO Interface nodes — measured 2026-09-16, scan_nodes Interface returns total 0 — even though the only thing the project delivers IS an interface. Every requirement and capability is phrased as a computation: "answer reference questions", "trace a beamline", "return plots". Not one says what a response must CARRY. With no contract, response shape was decided six separate times, by whoever wrote each return statement, with nothing to compare them against. That is the class behind four of the six trial findings: no version in any payload (F1), no timestamp (F2), inconsistent envelopes (F4), and — not noticed by the trial — two of the three tools it called have no output schema at all, so a model calling them cannot know what comes back until it arrives. The test that makes this a cause and not a description: fixing any one of F1, F2 or F4 on its own leaves the other two, and leaves the next tool free to invent a seventh convention.

properties.name: What the trial found WORKING — recorded so a later session does not optimise it away
properties.statement:
From the xrt-demo trial log, 2026-09-16, after three calls. Recorded because these are the things most at risk of being deleted by somebody tidying up, and one of them is load-bearing.

W1, LOAD-BEARING: two lines of the server instructions — that a geometric source is a stand-in for emission only, and that flux and power are within the sampled window so say which window you used — let the trial write an honest flux requirement BEFORE running a single trace. Its words: "a tool that tells you in advance which of its answers will be meaningless is doing something most tools do not. Keep both lines exactly as they are." Treat those two sentences as contract, not prose.

W2: units live in the key names throughout (d_spacing_A, bragg_angle_deg, darwin_width_urad, cutoff_energy_eV), and dimensionless quantities are named so. Across three tools the trial found no bare number whose unit it had to guess. Its design has a rule making an undeclared unit a finding, and it reports the server cannot currently produce one.

W3: crystal_at_energy returns the whole derivation — d-spacing, Bragg angle, Darwin width, dE/E, bandwidth — so the answer can be checked rather than trusted. It matched the brief to three figures (1.2267 vs 1.23 eV).

W4: mirror_cutoff carries its own definition in the payload ("highest energy where s-polarised reflectivity is still 50%"). The trial calls this rare and exactly right, and suggests extending it to other threshold-defined quantities — the FWHM convention on beam size, and what transmission is a fraction OF.

W5: list_beamlines descriptions say WHEN to use each template, not just what it is; the trial picked the right one without a second call.

Note the tension with the findings recorded beside this one: W2, W3 and W4 are all cases of a response carrying more than the bare answer, and F3 is a complaint that a response carried too much. Whoever settles the payload-budget question has to keep W3 and W4 while cutting F3, which means the cut is "make the bulk optional", not "return less".

properties.description: demo/run_demo.py, run for real against the server over stdio. Nine steps: crystal lookup, undulator harmonics, mirror cutoff, load the beamline, trace it, image the sample, image the beamline layout, scan the white-beam slit, detune the focusing mirror and trace again. A demonstration rather than a test: it asserts nothing, it produces the thing a beamline scientist is shown, and the check is whether the numbers and pictures are defensible.
properties.findings: Both modes ran clean on 2026-09-16. Real undulator, 9 keV: 3.36e15 ph/s and 4.85 W at the front end within the sampled window, falling to 4.92e13 ph/s in 27.5 x 4.3 um at 1.55 eV FWHM at the sample, 1.46% transmitted. The slit scan saturates around 1.0 mm, which is where the beam is fully accepted — visible in the curve, and the right shape. Detuning the mirror from 3.0 to 3.5 mrad grew the spot 22.6 -> 26.9 um, which is what a mirror no longer at the angle its radii were solved for should do. --fast finishes in about 15 seconds, the full undulator run in about two minutes.
properties.name: The demo run, end to end, both speeds

properties.description: tests/test_endtoend.py. Six tests that start the server as a subprocess and drive it with a genuine MCP client over stdio, rather than calling the Python functions underneath. They check that the tools list, that the crystal lookup matches textbook Si(111) values at 9 keV (Bragg 12.5-12.9 deg, bandwidth 1.0-1.5 eV), that a trace both monochromates (50 eV window down to under 4 eV) and focuses (millimetre beam down to under 80 x 20 um), that beam_image returns real PNG content, that opening a slit monotonically increases transmission, and that a wrong element name comes back as an explanation naming the real elements rather than as a stack trace. All use the geometric source, so the suite runs in about 23 seconds. What this catches that a unit test cannot: a tool whose signature the SDK cannot serialise fails here instead of in front of somebody.
properties.findings: 6 passed in 22.67s on 2026-09-16. One earlier failure was in the test, not the server: mcp 2.x names the field mime_type, not mimeType.
properties.name: End-to-end tests over the real MCP protocol

properties.description: tests/test_contract.py. Six tests, each written against the UNFIXED server and OBSERVED TO FAIL before anything was changed — all six failed on the first run, 2026-09-16. They pin the contract rather than the six reported instances: every evidence tool declares an output schema; every evidence tool carries a meta block; a default lookup reply stays under 2 KB and grows only when the curve is asked for; the reflectivity curve still shows Rh below its L edges at a value it does not recover to at 3500, 4200, 5000 or 8000 eV, which is the assertion that catches a re-decimation; the absorption edges are reported within 2% of the tabulated Rh L3/L2/L1 energies; and no continuous physical quantity is optional. The fourth is the one that matters most — it fails if anybody ever again samples a curve more coarsely than its own features.
properties.findings: 6 failed against the unfixed server, then 6 passed after the fix. Whole suite 16 passed in 68s on 2026-09-16, including the four slow undulator tests.
properties.name: The response contract, pinned

properties.description: tests/test_undulator_physics.py, marked slow. Four tests with real undulator emission. Tuning round-trips: solving K for an energy and asking where the harmonic sits returns the energy. An unreachable energy raises with the reason rather than silently picking a wrong K. Flux falls monotonically along the beamline and lands in a physically defensible range at the sample. And the decisive one: the Si(111) bandwidth predicted from the structure factor (1.23 eV at 9 keV) bounds the bandwidth that actually survives a trace from below, within a factor of six, because the incident divergence maps onto energy through cot(theta_B). That is two independent paths through the physics agreeing, which is the check a beamline scientist would ask for.
properties.name: Undulator physics, cross-checked two ways
